Empirical Research Plan  
“Do gubernatorial term limits change economic policy?”

------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
------------------------------------------------------------
Primary approach: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with staggered adoption plus an event-study.

Why it fits the question & data  
• The “treatment” (a binding gubernatorial term-limit) turns on and stays on in a subset of states that adopted limits—mostly by constitutional amendment or initiative—between the 1970s and the late-1990s.  
• Other states never adopted limits, giving us a clean control group.  
• We observe a long state-year panel containing fiscal policy outcomes, allowing us to difference out time-invariant state factors and common national shocks with two-way fixed effects.  
• An event-study around the adoption year lets us check pre-trends and measure dynamic effects.

Econometric form (TWFE compatible with recent corrections):  
Policy_st = Σ_k≠-1 β_k · 1{Year-Event = k}_st  +  X′_st γ  +  μ_s  +  λ_t  +  ε_st  
where μ_s are state FE and λ_t are year FE. We will implement Sun & Abraham (2021) / Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021) estimators to avoid bias from heterogeneous timing.

------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
BindLimit_st  = 1 if the incumbent governor in state s during year t is constitutionally barred from seeking immediate re-election because of a binding term-limit.  
(Instrumented later with the purely institutional indicator TermLimitLaw_st that equals 1 once the state constitution contains a limit, regardless of the individual governor’s tenure.)

Control group  
State-years in which the incumbent governor is eligible to run again, including (a) years before adoption in treated states and (b) all years in states that never adopt.

Treatment timing / event date  
Event_s  = first year the term-limit amendment becomes effective in state s.  
Event-time k = t − Event_s. We will keep observations from k = −10 to +10, dropping k = 0 to avoid perfect collinearity with the constant.

------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of term-limit adoption, fiscal policy in adopter states would have followed the same trend as in non-adopters.  
Plausibility: Term-limit adoptions were usually driven by voter initiatives rather than contemporaneous fiscal crises; yet policy preferences of states that chose limits might differ. We will probe this with pre-trend tests, state-specific linear trends, and propensity-score re-weighting.

A2. No anticipation: Governors do not change policy before the amendment becomes effective.  Plausible because amendments specify future effective dates and usually require a lag (first term after passage).

A3. Stable composition (no differential migration of states in/out of sample): High because U.S. states are fixed units; their boundaries and reporting rules hardly change.

A4. SUTVA / no spillovers: Policies in one state do not mechanically force changes in neighbors. Some interstate tax competition exists; we will add region-year fixed effects to mitigate.

------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats & Mitigation  
------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Political selection: Only politically successful governors make it to a (potentially term-limited) second term, biasing results.  
Remedy: Two-stage approach—instrument individual ineligibility with the state’s constitutional limit (First-stage F ≫ 10) and include governor FE wherever within-governor variation exists.

T2. Policy-driven adoption (reverse causality): Fiscal mismanagement might itself spur citizen initiatives for term limits.  
Remedy: (i) Event-study pre-trends; (ii) Include lags of fiscal variables as controls; (iii) Drop the 3 years immediately before the vote as a robustness check.

T3. Heterogeneous treatment timing bias in TWFE.  
Remedy: Use Sun & Abraham (2021) “interaction-weighted” estimator or Callaway-Sant’Anna (2021) group-time ATT implementation (did2s or fixest::feols + sunab()).

------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (executable)  
------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# install.packages(c("tidyverse","fixest","did","sandwich","modelsummary"))
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)     # fast FE + sunab()
library(did)        # Callaway–Sant'Anna ATT
library(modelsummary)

# 1. Load data -------------------------------------------------------------
dat <- read_csv("state_gov_policy.csv")  # assume wide state-year panel

# 2. Variable construction -------------------------------------------------
dat <- dat %>%
  mutate(
    # Term-limit law indicator: 1 once amendment effective
    TL_law = if_else(year >= tl_effective_year, 1, 0, missing = 0),

    # Incumbent eligibility (1 = cannot run again)
    TL_binding = if_else(TL_law == 1 & gov_term_number == max_terms_allowed, 1, 0),

    # Event time for Sun & Abraham
    event_time = if_else(TL_law == 1, year - tl_effective_year, NA_integer_)
  )

# 3. Main Sun & Abraham specification -------------------------------------
mod_main <- feols(
  policy_outcome ~ sunab(tl_effective_year, year) + controls... |
                   state + year,
  cluster = ~state,
  data = dat
)
etable(mod_main, dict = c("(Intercept)" = "Constant"))

# 4. Callaway & Sant’Anna robustness (did package) -------------------------
cs_att <- att_gt(yname = "policy_outcome",
                 tname = "year",
                 idname = "state",
                 gname = "tl_effective_year",
                 xformla = ~ controls...,
                 data = dat,
                 est_method = "dr")
agg_cs <- aggte(cs_att, type = "dynamic")
summary(agg_cs)

# 5. Simple 2-stage IV within adopters ------------------------------------
mod_iv <- feols(
  policy_outcome ~ TL_binding | state + year | TL_law ~ 1,
  cluster = ~state,
  data = dat %>% filter(year >= 1970)
)

# 6. Robustness check: drop 3 pre-adoption years --------------------------
dat_rb <- dat %>% filter(!(TL_law == 0 & year %in% (tl_effective_year - 3):(tl_effective_year - 1)))
mod_rb <- update(mod_main, data = dat_rb)

# 7. Present results -------------------------------------------------------
modelsummary(list(Main = mod_main, IV = mod_iv, NoPre = mod_rb),
             stars = TRUE, gof_omit = "Adj|R2")
```

------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
------------------------------------------------------------
Theory is ambiguous: loss of electoral discipline may (a) induce short-run patronage spending or (b) free the governor to enact politically costly but growth-enhancing reforms.

Empirical priors from the legislative-lame-duck literature suggest a modest shift toward higher spending and/or higher taxes. I expect:

β ≈ +1–2 % of total state expenditure (≈ 0.15σ of the dependent variable) during lame-duck years, with the effect materializing in the first two fiscal years after the limit binds.

------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Parallel pre-trends supported by event-study graphs .............. 0.8  
C2: No anticipation (checked by k = -2,-1 coefficients) ............... 0.9  
C3: No spillovers / SUTVA ............................................ 0.7  
C4: No time-varying composition or coding changes .................... 0.9  
C5: Correct inference (state-clustered SE, SA estimator) ............. 1.0  

Average ≈ 0.86 → mostly credible, but parallel-trend and spillover assumptions still need close scrutiny and robustness checks.

------------------------------------------------------------
End of research plan
